The Ghost of Hamlet's father appears in Hamlet as a spectre demanding vengeance, one of literature's most iconic supernatural figures. The ghost embodies the tragedy's central moral engine: Hamlet's uncertainty whether he is witnessing divine justice, demonic deception, or psychological hallucination, and the subsequent spiral into madness and violence triggered by his encounter with a perhaps-imaginary accuser.

The ghost appears first to the guards on the castle rampart, terrifying them with its physical presence and apparent distress, establishing an atmosphere of supernatural dread. It reveals to Hamlet that he was murdered by his brother Claudius while sleeping—poisoned through the ear—and demands revenge, cursing Claudius to eternal damnation. The method of murder is itself symbolic: a violation of the intimate passage through which one hears truth and receives communion, making it a peculiarly literary and psychological violation.

The ghost is never unambiguously confirmed as real. Hamlet's doubts about its authenticity drive the plot—hence the Mousetrap play to confirm Claudius's guilt. This reflects Renaissance uncertainty about spectral reality and demonic deception. The ghost appears again in Gertrude's bedroom, visible only to Hamlet. His mother cannot see it, deepening audience uncertainty about whether Hamlet is experiencing genuine supernatural contact or descent into madness.

The ghost represents the weight of paternal authority and obligation. Hamlet's inability to doubt or disobey it traps him in a predetermined revenge plot, raising questions about free will and filial duty. Modern psychology and criticism has interpreted the ghost as a manifestation of Hamlet's grief and ambivalence—projecting his superego as a spectral command, blaming his uncle for what may be his own inner conflict.

The ghost symbolizes the past's claim on the present. Its refusal to let Hamlet remain passive, insisting on action and violence, drives the tragedy's catastrophic final act.
